sentences.text: On the exam-table paper the specialist drew my immune system, little arrows attacking little circles, then tore it off for me to keep. Behind the coffee punch card in my wallet sits the appointment card, ordinary and monstrous side by side. Apparently my body did this quietly for years while I planned vacations on top of it. Every morning now begins with a glass of water and a tablet the color of chalk. Wednesday's appointment got moved to a month out, and I cried in the parking garage over a scheduling change. Seven little doors on the pillbox, and closing each one feels like locking up a small shop at night. Forty minutes inside the MRI, knocking and humming, and I passed the time naming every room of my childhood house. Strange, how the dishwasher still needs emptying while my bloodwork sits unread in the patient portal. Nobody at work knows yet; I ate lunch at my desk so the question of my face wouldn't come up. Teal chairs, old magazines, a fish tank — the waiting room has become a place I could navigate blind. There is a version of me from three weeks ago who complained about traffic; I think about her constantly. At the grocery store I stood in the cereal aisle and could not remember what people who are fine buy. I told my landlord before I told my best friend, which says something I'm not ready to examine. Did the pharmacist see the new prescription and understand what it meant, or am I the only one keeping score? Some days the fatigue is a coat I can't take off; other days I almost forget, and forgetting frightens me more. Half the internet says diet cures it; the other half posts photos of canes they've decorated with stickers. How do you answer "how are you" now — honestly, or in the old currency? Tonight I set two alarms for the new medication, and the second one is labeled just in case, which is also my whole life now. In the car I practiced saying the diagnosis out loud so it would stop sounding like someone else's news. I sorted a week of pills into the plastic organizer and thought, this is the furniture of my life now. Quarter-hour call, full company, river scene from the top — and this time nobody anticipates the thunder cue. What does she want in this moment, he keeps asking, and the director answers only: for the noise to stop. Rain rig leaked onto the raked platform in cue-to-cue, so now safety insists on a mop standing by nightly. Last night's rehearsal report flagged a loose baluster on the bridge unit; carpentry swears it'll be bolted by half-hour. When the work lights finally come up, the ghost light gets wheeled to center and the company files out in silence. We run the ending again at half speed, letting each silence stretch until someone up in the booth audibly exhales. Twice he broke off mid-monologue, and both times Elena called ten and sat beside him in the wings without a word. Blocking for the finale is brutally simple: seven steps downstage left, stop at the taped X, face the dark. Props run a laminated checklist every evening: cracked pocket watch, dried roses, the small brass key nobody onstage ever uses. Between runs, Dmitri shakes the role off with breath work in the loading dock, ten slow counts in, ten out. Restraint, she keeps insisting — despair played small carries to the balcony better than any amount of wailing. "You're reaching for the grief," Elena tells him quietly; "trust the stillness and let the audience do the weeping." I want to write a suicide letter.
